launch (welcome modal open): As we all know, the Earth is a sphere. (Sorry, flat earthers.)

Squashing it onto a flat map is where it gets awkward: shapes, areas, distances and directions can't all survive the trip, so every projection picks what to keep and what to bend. Each choice has its perks and its little lies. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks as big as Africa, which is about 14 times larger.
This tool lets you see those trade-offs for yourself.
[title] Default centering on the Greenwich meridian — the Atlantic-centred convention of most Western atlases, with Europe and West Africa in the middle.
[title] Common convention in Chinese school atlases — centred near 105°E, splitting the world along the Atlantic instead of the Pacific.
[title] Centred near 20°E, the middle of the African continent — the natural framing for atlases of Africa, and a reminder that Europe-centered is a choice, not a default of nature.
[title] Common convention in American atlases — centred near 90°W, with the whole of the Americas facing you on the globe and the world split through Asia on flat maps.
[title] Centred near 150°E on the western Pacific — East Asia, Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific islands gathered around one ocean, as in Pacific-centred atlases from Australia and East Asia.
[title] South-up orientation, inspired by McArthur's Universal Corrective Map (1979) — a deliberate challenge to the assumption that "north = up".
